newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung seen winning Hong Kong leadership vote.
newsitem.headline: Tung seen winning Hong Kong leadership vote.

text.p: Hong Kong's new elite gathered on Wednesday to select the leader-in-waiting in what is one of the most significant events in the British colony's long and often bumpy transition to Chinese rule in mid-1997.
The identity of the man destined to step into British Governor Chris Patten's shoes upon the handover next year is considered a foregone conclusion in Hong Kong.
Shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, 59, whose family empire was bailed out by China a decade ago, is expected to sweep effortlessly to victory.

Shanghai-born Tung grabbed 206 votes in the first round of voting last month. His nearest rival, former chief justice Yang Ti Liang, won 82 votes and the other leading contender, businessman Peter Woo, received 54.
Hong Kong newspapers predicted between 260 and 300 votes for Tung from the 400-member Selection Committee, which has been carefully assembled by Beijing.
He needs 201 votes during Wednesday's run-off to clinch victory and become Hong Kong's Chief Executive-designate.

The British colony's democratic lobby has dismissed the ballot as a travesty and boycotted the process. Pro-democracy activists staged an overnight vigil outside the Hong Kong conference centre where the balloting will take place.
Independent pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau plans to greet the incoming leader with a no-confidence debate in the Legislative Council later in the day.
China's official media hailed the selection process as the birth of true democracy in Hong Kong.

The Beijing-funded Ta Kung Pao said it was unprecedented in Hong Kong history for Hong Kong people to choose their leader and urged the colonial administration to ensure "troublemakers" could not disrupt the balloting.
Activists picketed the first round of voting last month presided over by China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who made his first visit to the British colony for the occasion.

"For the past 150 years, the governors appointed by Britain numbered more than 20-odd but did they ever consult the people of Hong Kong? Of course not," Qian told the panel seated in long rows before a raised dais in a scene similar to ceremonies in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
A survey by Hong Kong University on the eve of the poll showed 82.2 percent expected Tung to win, while 43.4 percent of respondents would back him if they had the chance to vote.
Yang would get 27.9 percent of popular support.
Sovereignty of Hong Kong, a tiny but wealthy community of 6.3 million people, reverts to China at midnight next June 30 -- 202 days from now.
